claims.text: TaVCrW is initially a disordered solid solution at 0 K.
The 0 K TaVCrW state may contain short-range order.
The MTP will be trained on GGA-PBE configurations spanning both solid and liquid TaVCrW phase space.
FEP will use the MTP as the reference potential and DFT as the target potential.
Replacing EAM and TI with MTP and FEP will reduce computational cost by more than 80%.
The MTP+FEP melting temperature will be within 10 K of the TOR-TILD result.
A supercell containing at least 128 atoms is sufficient to represent SRO without material finite-size effects.
The range 2000–2400 K covers the melting transition and relevant liquid configurations of TaVCrW.
Using finite-temperature DFT with the Mermin functional during data generation incorporates electronic-excitation effects into the training data.
The MTP can reproduce the ab initio liquid-phase distribution, including pair statistics and local coordination environments.
Accurate reproduction of the target phase-space distribution allows FEP to converge rapidly without a continuous TI path.
The MTP provides substantially faster energy and force evaluations than direct DFT.
A Bennett Acceptance Ratio or similar estimator can obtain the solid–liquid free-energy difference directly from MTP samples.
Training the MTP on the same electronic-structure physics as the baseline preserves the accuracy of the free-energy calculation.
SRO contributes a stabilization energy of approximately 2–3 meV/atom.
The proposed method will account for the electronic-excitation shift in the melting point.
The conventional TOR-TILD workflow requires extensive intermediate-state sampling and expensive DFT calculations.
Omitting a significant magnetic-entropy contribution may cause the model to underpredict liquid stability.
Underpredicting liquid stability would lead to an overestimated melting temperature.
GGA-PBE errors associated with V and Cr at 0 K may propagate to high-temperature local environments if those environments are not adequately represented in training.
